title: Insurance
objectives: Answer out loud: What's a combined ratio?

steps.body: Insurers collect premiums upfront and pay claims later. The money held in between is "float," invested for returns.
Like banks, they're valued on equity metrics: P/BV, P/E, plus ROE vs. cost of equity.

legend.meaning: Premium revenue recognized in the period

blocks.template: A combined ratio below {{1}} means an underwriting profit
The premiums held before claims are paid are called {{1}}

blocks.title: What's the combined ratio?
blocks.body:
(Claims + expenses) ÷ premiums earned. Below 100% means underwriting is profitable on its own; above 100% means the insurer relies on investment returns from the float.

**Interview answer:** "Claims plus expenses over premiums — under 100% means the insurer profits from underwriting before any investment income."

blocks.prompt: An insurer's combined ratio is 103%. What does that tell you?

options.text: It lost money on underwriting and relies on investment income from the float

blocks.explanation: Above 100% means claims plus expenses exceed premiums — underwriting loses money, so profit depends on investing the float.

blocks.title: Why does float matter?
blocks.teaser: The insurer invests money it will eventually pay out.
blocks.body: The insurer invests money it will eventually pay out. If underwriting breaks even, the float is effectively free capital. This is the core of Berkshire Hathaway's model.

blocks.title: Why are reserves a key risk?
blocks.teaser: Insurers estimate future claims and set aside reserves.
blocks.body: Insurers estimate future claims and set aside reserves. If those estimates are too low, they must take charges later that reduce book value.
